lessons.title: Sources of Damp: Rising Damp, Leaks, and Condensation
lessons.body: Damp is the enemy of any building. In Africa, we deal with three main types: rising damp, leaks, and condensation. Rising damp happens when ground water climbs up through porous walls by capillary action. You'll see a tide mark up to 1.5 meters high, white salt deposits, and peeling paint. It's common in older buildings without a damp-proof course (DPC). Leaks come from broken pipes, cracked roofs, or faulty gutters. They are often sudden and localized. Condensation occurs when warm, moist air meets a cold surface, like a cold wall or window. In humid areas like the coast, condensation can cause mould and mildew. To identify the source, check for patterns: rising damp is continuous along the base, leaks are patchy and may drip, condensation appears on cold surfaces and disappears when ventilated. Use a moisture meter (cost about $30) to measure. A simple test: tape a square of aluminium foil to the wall for 24 hours. If moisture appears on the outside, it's condensation; if on the inside, it's rising damp or a leak. Fixing the source is the first step before any waterproofing.

lessons.title: Installing Damp-Proof Courses
lessons.body: A damp-proof course (DPC) is a barrier that stops moisture from rising up through walls. In Africa, we use materials like bitumen felt, plastic sheets (polyethylene), or slate. For existing buildings, you can install a DPC by cutting a horizontal slot into the wall about 150mm above ground level, using a angle grinder or masonry saw. The slot should be about 12mm wide and deep enough to go through the wall. Then insert a DPC membrane, such as a 0.5mm thick polyethylene sheet, and seal it with mortar. For new construction, place the DPC between the foundation and the first course of bricks. Ensure it's continuous and overlaps at corners. Cost: about $2 per meter for polyethylene. Tools: angle grinder, mortar, trowel, DPC membrane. Safety: wear goggles and gloves. After installation, replaster the wall. This method can last 20-30 years if done correctly. If you can't cut a slot, you can inject a chemical DPC (silane/siloxane) into holes drilled every 150mm. This is more expensive but less invasive.

lessons.title: Using Waterproof Membranes and Coatings
lessons.body: Waterproof membranes and coatings are your second line of defence after fixing the source. For roofs, use bituminous membranes (torch-on) or EPDM rubber. For walls, cementitious coatings (like Thoroseal) are popular in Africa because they are affordable and easy to apply. First, clean the surface: remove loose paint, dirt, and mould with a wire brush and water. Let it dry. Mix the coating according to the instructions (usually 1 part water to 3 parts powder). Apply two coats with a brush or roller, waiting 4-6 hours between coats. Coverage: 1kg covers about 1 square meter per coat. For extra protection, embed a fibreglass mesh into the first coat. For below-ground walls, use a bituminous coating or a dimpled drainage membrane. For flat roofs, use a polyurethane coating. Cost: cementitious coating is about $5 per kg; bitumen is $3 per kg. Always apply when rain is not expected for 24 hours. Temperature should be between 10Â°C and 35Â°C. Ventilate the area. These coatings can last 5-10 years if maintained.

lessons.title: Improving Drainage Around Buildings
lessons.body: Water pooling around your foundation is a major cause of damp. Improve drainage by creating a slope away from the building. The ground should fall at least 150mm over the first 3 meters (a 5% slope). If you have a garden, dig a swale (a shallow ditch) 300mm deep and 600mm wide, lined with gravel, to channel water away. For downspouts, extend them at least 1.5 meters from the wall using plastic pipes. Install a French drain: dig a trench 300mm wide and 600mm deep around the perimeter, fill with 20mm gravel, and lay a perforated pipe at the bottom. Cover with geotextile fabric to prevent clogging. Slope the pipe 1% towards a soakaway or storm drain. In areas with heavy rain, consider a soakaway pit: a 1m x 1m x 1m hole filled with rubble, allowing water to seep into the ground. Cost: about $50 for a 10-meter French drain. Tools: shovel, wheelbarrow, level, gravel. Clean gutters regularly to prevent overflow. These simple steps can reduce damp significantly.

lessons.title: Ventilation Strategies to Reduce Moisture
lessons.body: Good ventilation removes moist air before it causes condensation. In Africa, many buildings rely on natural ventilation, but you can improve it. Install air bricks (also called vents) in walls, especially in kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry areas. A 215mm x 65mm air brick provides about 1000mmÂ² of free area. Place them low and high to create cross-ventilation. For rooms with poor airflow, use extractor fans: a 100mm fan can move 80 cubic meters per hour. Cost: $20-$50. In humid coastal areas, use dehumidifiers or ceiling fans to circulate air. Open windows for at least 15 minutes a day, even in the rainy season. For roofs, ensure eaves are ventilated with soffit vents. If you have a crawl space, install vents every 2 meters. Avoid blocking vents with furniture or plants. For traditional buildings, use thatch or breathable materials. A simple trick: place a bowl of salt or charcoal in damp corners to absorb moisture. But ventilation is more effective. Regular maintenance: check vents for blockages, clean fans, and ensure doors have gaps for air movement.

lessons.title: Practical: Applying a Waterproof Coating to a Wall
lessons.body: In this practical, you will apply a cementitious waterproof coating to a damp wall. Tools: wire brush, trowel, bucket, measuring jug, mixing paddle, paintbrush, roller, gloves, goggles. Materials: cementitious coating powder (e.g., Thoroseal), water, fibreglass mesh (optional). Step 1: Prepare the surface. Remove all loose paint, dirt, and efflorescence with a wire brush. Rinse with water and let dry. Step 2: Mix the coating. Add 1 part clean water to 3 parts powder in a bucket. Mix with a paddle until smooth and lump-free. Let it sit for 5 minutes. Step 3: Apply the first coat. Dampen the wall with water. Apply a thin, even coat using a brush or roller. Work it into the surface. If using mesh, embed it while the coating is wet. Step 4: Wait 4-6 hours (or as per instructions) until the first coat is touch-dry. Step 5: Apply the second coat at right angles to the first. Step 6: Cure the coating. Keep it damp for 24 hours by misting with water. Avoid rain for 48 hours. Clean tools with water immediately. Cost: for a 10mÂ² wall, you need about 20kg of coating, costing $100. This coating will stop damp and protect the wall for years.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of rising damp?
options: B) Ground water rising through walls by capillary action
quiz.explanation: Rising damp occurs when ground water climbs up through porous walls by capillary action.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of rising damp?
options: B) White salt deposits on lower walls
quiz.explanation: White salt deposits and a tide mark up to 1.5m are typical signs of rising damp.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for a damp-proof course (DPC) above ground?
quiz.explanation: A DPC is typically installed about 150mm above ground level to prevent rising damp.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used as a DPC in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Bitumen felt, polythene sheet, and slate are all used as DPC materials in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the first step before applying a waterproof coating?
quiz.explanation: The surface must be clean, free of loose paint and dirt, for the coating to adhere properly.

quiz.q: How many coats of cementitious waterproof coating are usually applied?
quiz.explanation: Two coats are standard, with the second applied at right angles to the first.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a French drain?
options: A) To collect rainwater from the roof
B) To channel water away from the building foundation
C) To store water for dry season
quiz.explanation: A French drain is a trench filled with gravel and a perforated pipe that redirects groundwater away from the foundation.

quiz.q: What slope should the ground have away from a building?
quiz.explanation: A 5% slope (150mm fall over 3 meters) ensures water flows away from the building.

quiz.q: Which of these is a ventilation strategy to reduce moisture?
options: C) Using plastic sheets on walls
quiz.explanation: Air bricks allow cross-ventilation, removing moist air from the building.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size of an air brick?
quiz.explanation: A standard air brick is 215mm x 65mm, providing about 1000mmÂ² of free area.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to distinguish condensation from rising damp?
options: B) Tape aluminium foil to the wall for 24 hours
C) Pour water on the wall
quiz.explanation: If moisture appears on the outside of the foil, it's condensation; if inside, it's rising damp or a leak.

quiz.q: What is the cost of a moisture meter mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: A basic moisture meter costs about $30 and helps identify damp sources.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used for injectable DPC?
quiz.explanation: Silane/siloxane is injected into drilled holes to create a chemical DPC.

quiz.q: How long should you wait between coats of cementitious coating?
quiz.explanation: The first coat should be touch-dry, typically after 4-6 hours, before applying the second.

quiz.q: What is the coverage of 1kg of cementitious coating per coat?
quiz.explanation: 1kg covers about 1 square meter per coat, depending on surface porosity.

quiz.q: What is a soakaway pit?
options: A) A pit for storing water
B) A hole filled with rubble to allow water to seep into the ground
C) A tank for rainwater harvesting
quiz.explanation: A soakaway pit is a 1m x 1m x 1m hole filled with rubble that collects and disperses water underground.

quiz.q: How far should downspouts extend from the wall?
quiz.explanation: Extending downspouts at least 1.5 meters from the wall prevents water from pooling near the foundation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of geotextile fabric in a French drain?
options: B) To prevent soil from clogging the gravel
quiz.explanation: Geotextile fabric allows water through but keeps soil out, preventing clogging.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for a French drain pipe?
quiz.explanation: A 1% slope (1cm per meter) ensures water flows towards the soakaway.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural ventilation method?
quiz.explanation: Air bricks are a passive, natural ventilation method.

quiz.q: How often should you open windows to ventilate a room?
quiz.explanation: Opening windows for at least 15 minutes daily helps remove moist air.

quiz.q: What is the cost of a 100mm extractor fan?
quiz.explanation: A basic 100mm extractor fan costs between $20 and $50.

quiz.q: What is the first step in applying a waterproof coating?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the surface removes loose material and ensures adhesion.

quiz.q: What is the mixing ratio for cementitious coating?
options: A) 1 part water to 1 part powder
B) 1 part water to 3 parts powder
C) 3 parts water to 1 part powder
D) 1 part water to 5 parts powder
quiz.explanation: The typical ratio is 1 part clean water to 3 parts powder by volume.

quiz.q: How long should you cure the coating by keeping it damp?
quiz.explanation: Curing for 24 hours by misting with water ensures proper strength development.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of materials for a 10mÂ² wall?
quiz.explanation: About 20kg of coating is needed, costing around $100.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a source of damp?
quiz.explanation: Sunlight dries moisture; it is not a source of damp.

quiz.q: What is efflorescence?
options: A) White salt deposits on walls
quiz.explanation: Efflorescence is the white, powdery salt deposit left when water evaporates from masonry.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth of a French drain trench?
quiz.explanation: A French drain trench is typically 600mm deep and 300mm wide.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a DPC?
options: A) To stop water rising through walls
quiz.explanation: A damp-proof course is a barrier that prevents moisture from rising up through walls by capillary action.
